clue.text: Fielding's version of this Moliere character was by definition close

definitions.text: Fielding's version of this Moliere character was by definition close

parts.words: Fielding's version of this Moliere character was by definition close
parts.note: Henry Fielding adapted Moliere's L'Avare for the English stage; its title figure is tight-fisted, and close means stingy

explanation.surface: A literary note on how Fielding rendered one of Moliere's figures.
explanation.walkthrough: Fielding's 1733 comedy was an English version of Moliere's L'Avare; 'close' here means mean with money, the trait that defines the character.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarder of money who will not spend is the stingy title figure of both comedies.

clue.text: War novelist anyhow ran to arms

indicators.note: anyhow means in no particular order, so the letters of ran to arms are jumbled

explanation.surface: A soldier-writer dashed off to take up weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' rearranges RANTOARMS. Nicholas Monsarrat wrote The Cruel Sea, a novel of the Second World War at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Monsarrat is best known for The Cruel Sea, a naval novel of the Second World War.

clue.text: Scene of puzzle provided by Erskine Childers

definitions.text: Scene of puzzle provided by Erskine Childers

parts.words: Scene of puzzle provided by Erskine Childers
parts.note: Childers wrote The Riddle of the ..., a spy novel set among the shoals of the Frisian coast; riddle is the puzzle

explanation.surface: A question about where Erskine Childers set a mystery.
explanation.walkthrough: Childers's 1903 novel The Riddle of the Sands is set among tidal flats off the German coast; 'puzzle' stands for 'Riddle'.
explanation.definitionFit: The tidal flats and shoals off the Frisian coast are where the riddle of that novel unfolds.

clue.text: 24 painter well versed in French customs

definitions.meaning: 24 is the answer to 24-down, an artist without formal training, so this is the best-known such painter
Henri ... worked in the Paris toll office and was nicknamed le Douanier, the customs man

explanation.surface: A self-taught artist who knew all about French customs.
explanation.walkthrough: '24' points to 24-down, NAIVE. Henri Rousseau, the naive painter, was a customs official, hence le Douanier; 'customs' looks like traditions.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Rousseau, the self-taught painter of jungles, earned his living at the Paris octroi, a toll and customs post.

clue.text: Scot in a very quiet thoroughfare near Rome

indicators.note: in tells us the Scottish name is placed inside the other pieces

parts.note: pp, pianissimo, is the musical marking for very quiet
a way is a road or thoroughfare
Ian is a typical Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A Scotsman walking along a hushed road outside Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thoroughfare' does double service, giving its synonym and heading the definition of the ancient road leading south-east out of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The Via Appia is the ancient Roman road running south-east from the city.

clue.text: Puts a question to initiate all scientific knowledge somehow Philosopher retraces Argosy path

indicators.note: initiate here means taking the opening letters, the initials of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Someone queries whether all scientific knowledge begins somehow.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letters of 'all scientific knowledge somehow' spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To query someone is to put a question to them.

clue.text: Philosopher retraces Argosy path

indicators.note: retraces suggests going over again in a new way, so the letters of Argosy path are rearranged

explanation.surface: A thinker follows again the route of the Argo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retraces' rearranges ARGOSYPATH; the Argo's voyage is the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Pythagoras of Samos was a Greek thinker and mathematician of the sixth century BC.

clue.text: Closed communities for persons with similar habits

definitions.text: Closed communities for persons with similar habits

parts.words: Closed communities for persons with similar habits
parts.note: habits are the robes worn by monks and nuns, who live apart in enclosed religious houses

explanation.surface: Gated estates for people who share the same routines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'habits' means monastic robes, not routines; the closed communities are enclosed religious houses.
explanation.definitionFit: Monasteries and convents house monks or nuns who all wear the same robes.

clue.text: London dog

parts.note: Jack London wrote a novel about a wolf-dog of the Yukon

explanation.surface: A hound from the British capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'London' is Jack London the American author, not the city; his 1906 novel is named after its wolf-dog hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The wolf-dog hero of Jack London's 1906 novel of the Klondike gives the book its title.

clue.text: Rumoured youthful author of The Trial

indicators.note: rumoured means reported by word of mouth, so we want a word heard rather than seen

parts.note: youthful means young

explanation.surface: A whisper that the writer of The Trial was young.
explanation.walkthrough: The Trial is not Kafka's here but Charlotte Yonge's 1864 novel; 'Rumoured' signals that her surname sounds like YOUNG.
explanation.definitionFit: Charlotte Mary Yonge, the Victorian novelist, wrote The Trial as a sequel to The Daisy Chain.

clue.text: A starting point for Melville

parts.note: Ishmael sails on the Pequod from a Massachusetts whaling island in Moby-Dick

explanation.surface: Where one might begin reading Melville.
explanation.walkthrough: In Moby-Dick, Ishmael and Queequeg set out on the Pequod from this whaling island off Massachusetts.
explanation.definitionFit: The island off Cape Cod was the whaling port from which the Pequod sails in Moby-Dick.

clue.text: "Has he not well provided for the —?" (Beaumont and Fletcher, Love's Cure)

definitions.text: "Has he not well provided for the —?" (Beaumont and Fletcher, Love's Cure)

parts.words: "Has he not well provided for the —?" (Beaumont and Fletcher, Love's Cure)
parts.note: the missing word in this line from the Jacobean comedy is the Scots word for a child

explanation.surface: A quotation from a Jacobean comedy with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the gap in the quotation; the missing word is the Scottish and northern English word for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scots term for a young child, the offspring someone has provided for.

clue.text: Town in pass is instantly recognized as bird sanctuary

indicators.note: in tells us the answer sits inside the words pass is instantly

explanation.surface: A town is at once known as a haven for birds.
explanation.walkthrough: The town lies within 'pass is instantly'. 'recognized as bird sanctuary' alludes to St Francis of Assisi, who preached to the birds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Umbrian hill town in Italy is the birthplace of St Francis, patron of animals.

clue.text: Rosalind the cup-bearer?

definitions.meaning: in As You Like It, Rosalind disguises herself as a youth and takes a boy's name
the Trojan boy carried off by Zeus to pour wine for the gods on Olympus

explanation.surface: Is Shakespeare's heroine the one who serves the drinks?
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's heroine takes this name in disguise in Arden, the name of the Trojan youth who served wine to the gods.

clue.text: An alter ego to conceal, say, with teddy

parts.note: Teddy is a pet form of the name Edward

indicators.note: say signals a word as it is heard rather than as it is spelt

parts.note: to conceal means to hide

explanation.surface: A second self hides behind a teddy bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the pieces. 'teddy' looks like a bear but is a nickname for Edward; 'say' makes HIDE sound like Jekyll's other self.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's tale, Dr Jekyll's monstrous other self goes by this name.

clue.text: Paladin's boy, we are told, is an illustrator

indicators.note: we are told signals that the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: Roland was the chief paladin of Charlemagne, so his boy is Roland's son

explanation.surface: Gossip says the knight's son draws pictures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' links. Thomas Rowlandson was a Georgian caricaturist; Roland was Charlemagne's foremost paladin.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Rowlandson was an English caricaturist and draughtsman of the Georgian era.

clue.text: Dickens notary seen to waste study

parts.note: to waste away is to wither
a den is a private room for study

explanation.surface: A lawyer in Dickens is seen letting his study go to ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seen to' links. Mr Witherden is the notary in The Old Curiosity Shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Witherden is the lawyer to whom Abel Garland is articled in The Old Curiosity Shop.

clue.text: Brandy associated with Chagall

definitions.meaning: a spirit distilled from grape skins left after wine-pressing
the first name of the Russian-French painter Chagall

explanation.surface: A spirit linked with a Russian-born painter.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both the spirit distilled from grape pomace and the painter Chagall's first name.

clue.text: One boy in exact copy of enamel work

indicators.note: in tells us the first pieces are placed inside the copy

parts.note: a clone is an exact copy
one is the Roman numeral I
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A lad who is the spitting image of an enamelled ornament.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloisonne is decorative enamelling set in compartments formed by thin metal strips.

clue.text: Comic writer from Arab isle

indicators.note: from suggests the answer is made out of the letters of Arab isle

explanation.surface: A humorous author hails from an island in Arabia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' tells us to make the answer out of the letters of ARABISLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Francois Rabelais was the French Renaissance satirist who wrote Gargantua and Pantagruel.

clue.text: Doubly intimate French skirt

indicators.note: doubly means the piece appears twice in a row

parts.note: tu is the familiar French word for you

explanation.surface: A doubly close French garment.
explanation.walkthrough: French uses 'tu' for 'you' only with intimates; twice gives the ballet skirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutu is the stiff short skirt worn by ballerinas.

clue.text: A vicar, agog, upset refugee artist

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of a vicar agog are rearranged

explanation.surface: An excited vicar is agitated by a painter in exile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges AVICARAGOG. Caravaggio fled Rome in 1606 after killing a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Caravaggio spent his final years fleeing a murder charge, moving from Naples to Malta and Sicily.

clue.text: Playwright as devout emperor

parts.note: pi is short for pious, meaning devout
Nero was a Roman emperor

explanation.surface: A dramatist who is as pious as a Roman ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' links. Arthur Wing Pinero wrote farces such as The Magistrate.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Wing Pinero was a late Victorian English dramatist, author of The Second Mrs Tanqueray.

clue.text: Hitchcock's take on Greek comedy?

parts.note: Hitchcock's 1963 thriller shares its title with a comedy by Aristophanes

explanation.surface: Wondering whether Hitchcock adapted an ancient Greek play.
explanation.walkthrough: Aristophanes wrote a comedy of this name; Hitchcock's 1963 horror film of feathered attackers shares it, though from Daphne du Maurier.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the 1963 Hitchcock thriller and Aristophanes' comedy of Cloudcuckooland have this title.

clue.text: Path of Walpole's master, say?

indicators.note: say signals the name as heard rather than spelt

parts.note: in Hugh Walpole's novel Mr Perrin and Mr Traill, the second schoolmaster is named Traill

explanation.surface: A question about the route taken by Walpole's teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: The Walpole is Hugh, not Horace or Robert: his school novel's young master Mr Traill sounds like the word for a track.
explanation.definitionFit: A trail is a track or way worn through the country.

clue.text: Second of two writers identifying Thackeray work

definitions.text: Second of two writers identifying Thackeray work

parts.words: Second of two writers identifying Thackeray work
parts.note: Thackeray's novel ... splits into PEN, a writer

explanation.surface: A remark about the second of a pair of authors naming a Thackeray novel.
explanation.walkthrough: PEN, a writer, followed by the critic John Dennis gives Thackeray's Pendennis; the answer is the second of the two.
explanation.definitionFit: John Dennis was an Augustan critic, and joined to a pen his name makes Thackeray's novel Pendennis.

clue.text: Innocent as le Carré' lover

definitions.meaning: le Carre wrote The ... and Sentimental Lover

explanation.surface: Guileless like a romantic in a le Carre novel.
explanation.definitionFit: It means unworldly or green, and is the first adjective in the title of le Carre's novel The Naive and Sentimental Lover.

clue.text: Final solution in Egypt as afterthought

parts.note: PS, postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: Cleopatra's last resort, mentioned as a postscript.
explanation.walkthrough: Cleopatra ended her life with the bite of a venomous snake, hence the 'final solution in Egypt'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra is said to have killed herself with venomous snakes, her last way out in Egypt.

clue.text: "Poor slaves in metre, dull and — pated" (Dryden)

definitions.text: "Poor slaves in metre, dull and — pated" (Dryden)

parts.words: "Poor slaves in metre, dull and — pated" (Dryden)
parts.note: the missing word in Dryden's line combines with pated to mean muddle-headed

explanation.surface: A line of Dryden on dull versifiers, with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the gap: '-pated' compounds mean '-headed', and the missing word means confused, giving muddle-headed.
explanation.definitionFit: To confuse or muddle; with -pated it makes a word for muddle-headed.

clue.text: Determined to "live for ever or die in the attempt", he found a catch in it

definitions.text: Determined to "live for ever or die in the attempt", he found a catch in it

parts.words: Determined to "live for ever or die in the attempt", he found a catch in it
parts.note: the bombardier hero of Joseph Heller's Catch-22 resolves to live for ever or die in the attempt

explanation.surface: A man set on immortality discovers a snag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'catch' points to Catch-22, Heller's novel, whose hero vowed to live for ever or die in the attempt.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Yossarian is the bombardier at the centre of Joseph Heller's Catch-22.

clue.text: Some capital characters from Maureen Duffy

definitions.text: Some capital characters from Maureen Duffy

parts.words: Some capital characters from Maureen Duffy
parts.note: Maureen Duffy wrote a 1983 novel named after inhabitants of the English capital

explanation.surface: A few important figures from a Maureen Duffy novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like 'excellent' but means the capital city; Maureen Duffy's novel is named after its residents.
explanation.definitionFit: Maureen Duffy's 1983 novel takes its title from residents of the British capital, who are its characters.

clue.text: Shaw's investment

definitions.meaning: Irwin Shaw wrote a 1937 play of this name about the Spanish Civil War
investment in the military sense is the surrounding of a town by an army

explanation.surface: Where Shaw put his money.
explanation.definitionFit: Investment in its military sense is the blockading of a fortified place, and Irwin Shaw's 1937 play bears this title.
